```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 8, fig.height = 6)
set.seed(123)
```

## 1. Question and data

**Question:** does BCG vaccination reduce the risk of tuberculosis, and does the
effect differ between studies?

**Data:** the classic `dat.bcg` dataset shipped with the `metafor` package
(Colditz et al. 1994): 13 randomized or quasi-randomized trials. For each trial
it reports the number of tuberculosis cases and non-cases in the vaccinated
(`tpos`, `tneg`) and control (`cpos`, `cneg`) groups, plus the absolute latitude
of the study site (`ablat`) and the allocation method (`alloc`).

This project covers the **statistical meta-analysis** step. It does not include
a literature search, screening or risk-of-bias assessment.

```{r libs}
library(metafor)
```

```{r data}
dat.bcg
```

## 2. Effect sizes

The effect measure is the log risk ratio (vaccinated vs control). A value below
zero means fewer cases among the vaccinated.

```{r escalc}
dat <- escalc(measure = "RR", ai = tpos, bi = tneg, ci = cpos, di = cneg,
              data = dat.bcg)
dat$study <- paste(dat$author, dat$year, sep = ", ")
dat[, c("study", "yi", "vi")]
```

## 3. Random-effects meta-analysis

A random-effects model (REML) allows the true effect to differ between trials.

```{r rma}
res <- rma(yi, vi, data = dat, method = "REML", slab = dat$study)
summary(res)

# Pooled estimate back-transformed to a risk ratio
predict(res, transf = exp, digits = 2)
```

## 4. Forest plot

```{r forest}
forest(res, atransf = exp, at = log(c(0.05, 0.25, 1, 4)),
       header = TRUE, xlab = "Risk ratio (log scale)")
```

## 5. Heterogeneity

`tau^2` is the between-study variance, `I^2` the percentage of total variability
due to heterogeneity, and `Q` tests whether the trials share one true effect.

```{r het}
data.frame(tau2 = res$tau2, I2 = res$I2, H2 = res$H2,
           Q = res$QE, Q_pvalue = res$QEp)

# Prediction interval on the risk-ratio scale
predict(res, transf = exp, digits = 2)
```

## 6. Publication bias

```{r bias}
funnel(res)
regtest(res)            # Egger-type regression test
trimfill(res)           # trim-and-fill adjusted estimate
```

## 7. Sensitivity: leave-one-out

```{r l1o}
l1 <- leave1out(res, transf = exp)
out <- data.frame(omitted = dat$study, as.data.frame(l1)[, c("estimate", "ci.lb", "ci.ub", "I2")])
out
```

## 8. Explaining heterogeneity: moderators

Absolute latitude is a known moderator of BCG efficacy. A meta-regression tests
whether the effect changes with latitude.

```{r mod}
res.lat <- rma(yi, vi, mods = ~ ablat, data = dat, method = "REML")
summary(res.lat)

regplot(res.lat, mod = "ablat", xlab = "Absolute latitude",
        ylab = "Log risk ratio")
```

Allocation method as a categorical moderator:

```{r alloc}
res.alloc <- rma(yi, vi, mods = ~ factor(alloc), data = dat, method = "REML")
res.alloc
```

## 9. Export

```{r export}
dir.create("results", showWarnings = FALSE)
write.csv(dat[, c("study", "yi", "vi")], "results/effect_sizes.csv", row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(out, "results/leave_one_out.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

## 10. Limitations

- Only 13 trials, so tests for heterogeneity, publication bias and moderators have
  limited power.
- Funnel-plot methods are unreliable with fewer than about 10 studies.
- Latitude is a study-level variable, so the meta-regression is an association
  across trials, not proof of a causal mechanism.
- This project does not cover study identification, screening or risk-of-bias
  assessment (the PRISMA steps).
